Thank you for helping us improve the manuscript.

“l.305 "has the expected error of approximately [...]" I am unsure where this statement comes from, could the authors clarify?”

In Section 5.1, the phrase “the expected error of approximately” refers to a widely used approximation based on the so-called “universality assumption”, a term adopted in the eigen-learning framework of Simon et al. (TMLR 2023). We provide further details on this assumption in our response to reviewer HVtJ, where we addressed the question related to line 305.

“why the error of conditional KRR corresponds to the error of KRR with the residual kernel plus the conditioning cost (l.307)?”




The cost of conditioning quantifies the squared $L_2$-distance between the estimator produced by C-KRR and the estimator obtained from $\mathcal{F}$-conditional learning. In subsection 5.1, we assume that the regression function lies in $\mathcal{F}$. Under this assumption, $\mathcal{F}$-conditional learning is, by definition, equivalent to applying standard KRR with the residual kernel to a dataset consisting only of noise, $\{(X_i, \varepsilon_i)\}_{i=1}^N$. This immediately yields that the expected risk of C-KRR is bounded by the expected risk of this noise-only KRR plus the cost of conditioning.

This reasoning also clarifies why we use the term “cost of conditioning”. Once we account for $c_{\rm con}$, we can view C-KRR as essentially equivalent to standard KRR with kernel $K_P$ applied to a pure-noise dataset---

C-KRR with kernel $K \approx$ KRR with kernel $K_P$ (modulo the $\mathcal{F}$-component),

at the expense of adding $c_{\rm con}$ to the expected risk.



“I am unsure how the second statement follows from (3), notably the ascending part of the U. ”

Standard KRR (with the original kernel $K$) corresponds to C-KRR with $k = 0$. Therefore, condition (3) guarantees that

The expected risk of C-KRR for given $k$ < The expected risk of C-KRR for $k=0$

This means that the expected risk decreases when we increase the number of unpenalized modes from $0$ to a given $k$. Since the expected risk typically cannot continue decreasing indefinitely as $k$ grows (due to overfitting), it must typically exhibit a U-shaped dependence on $k$.



“To the best of my reading, the authors contrast KRR and conditional KRR with the same regularization \lambda”

Yes, in our analysis in Section 5.1 we assume that the regularization parameter $\lambda$ is fixed; we do not assume access to an optimally tuned $\lambda$. In the revised manuscript, we have added experiments comparing C-KRR with KRR optimized over $\lambda$. Since this question was also raised by two previous reviewers, we refer to our response to Weakness 2 from reviewer oQxu.

We appreciate your thoughtful comments and have addressed the issues you raised in the updated version of the manuscript.

Q1: “Why is it important to develop a statistical theory of learning for conditional KRR?”

We emphasize that solving the regression problem by minimizing objective (1) --- what we call conditional KRR --- is not a new method. It has been used for roughly three decades (as noted in the citations in the first paragraph), so developing its statistical theory is valuable even for deepening our understanding of this classical approach. Another motivation comes from questions such as: if we simply memorize the residuals left after a basic training method (e.g., the “ResMem: Learn What You Can and Memorize the Rest” paper, NeurIPS 2023), what level of performance can be achieved?

W1: “It would be nice to empirically see a relevant setting (or, at least, any setting at all) in which conditional KRR outperforms optimally-regularized KRR”

We have updated the manuscript, marking all additions in red. In these revisions, we demonstrate several cases where C-KRR outperforms standard KRR. Since the same concern was raised by reviewer oQxu, we refer you to our response to Weakness 2 in the previous discussion thread.

W3: “The proposed quantity "cost of conditioning" seems like a misnomer, and it's not clear how to interpret it.”

A key observation is that the statistical behavior of conditional KRR can be reduced to that of standard KRR; this is precisely the content of Theorem 4. We analyze a standard KRR as if the $\mathcal{F}$-component of the regression function were known, and we show that its output is close to that of conditional KRR. Crucially, this KRR uses a fixed kernel (the residual kernel defined by the true distribution $P$, not by the empirical data). Since the kernel is fixed, the extensive theoretical toolbox available for standard KRR becomes applicable.

The gap between the two outputs is what we call “the cost of conditioning”: it represents the additional expected risk incurred when replacing conditional KRR with an equivalent standard KRR that assumes knowledge of the $\mathcal{F}$-component. Through Theorem 4, any theoretical result established for standard KRR (many deep results exist, especially those relying on kernel spectra) can be turned into a nontrivial statement about conditional KRR, with the cost of conditioning added. Thus, this cost refers to the theoretical overhead of reducing the statistical analysis of C-KRR to that of standard KRR with a fixed kernel, rather than simply the numerical distance between their outputs.

Let us address the weakness W5: “I believe there is an error in line 305 -- the test error should not vanish when the target noise vanishes. There will be leftover estimator variance from the sampling noise.”
In the following remark we also address the question of a reviewer pVbK: “l.305 "has the expected error of approximately [...]" I am unsure where this statement comes from, could the authors clarify?”

Thank you for highlighting this interesting point. However, there is no inconsistency once the statements are interpreted within the “eigen-framework for KRR generalization”, the terminology you yourself used. Recall that this framework relies on the “universality assumption”, which posits that for a finite sample ${X_i}_{i=1}^N \sim P$, the design matrix

$$
[\phi_j(X_i)]_{1 \le i \le N,1 \le j \le k}
$$

behaves like a matrix with i.i.d. standard normal entries. In slightly different language, this assumption appeared earlier as the “Gaussianity assumption” in Section 2.4 of Jacot et al., Kernel Alignment Risk Estimator (NIPS 2020). It has since become widely used in recent theoretical analyses of KRR (e.g., Mallinar et al., NeurIPS 2022; Simon et al., ICLR 2024), because the resulting formulas match empirical behavior not only qualitatively but also quantitatively. Our expected-risk calculations are based on this same assumption.

In Section 5.1, we assume that the regression function has the form
$$
f = \sum_{j=1}^k u_j \phi_j.
$$
When $\sigma^2 = 0$, the outputs for sampled inputs 

$\{X_i\}_{i=1}^N \sim P$ 

satisfy 

$y = \{f(X_i)\}_{i=1}^N = X u,$

where
$$
X = [\phi_j(X_i)]_{1 \le i \le N, 1 \le j \le k}
$$
and $u = (u_1,\ldots,u_k)^\top$.
As soon as $N \ge k$, the matrix $X$ has rank $k$ with probability 1, which implies that the coefficients $u_j$ can be recovered exactly from $(X, y)$. In this case, the expected risk indeed becomes zero.

Recovering the coefficients $u_j$ exactly is also not unrealistic. Since we assume that the support of the distribution $P$ coincides with the full domain $\mathcal{X}$, the design matrix fails to be full rank only in practically exceptional cases. For example, even on a finite domain $\mathcal{X}$, there is always a nonzero probability that $X$ is not full rank, but in practice this probability is negligible.

Let me address the first comment first.
The claim that “$X$ is full rank” is valid under the “universality assumption”, since under this assumption the entries of $X$ are i.i.d. standard normal. That is why $\mathcal{E}' = 0$ holds in the noiseless case. Many theoretical papers rely on the Gaussianity assumption because it leads to simple formulas that agree with numerical experiments both qualitatively and quantitatively. The drawback, however, is that this assumption never holds perfectly in practice (even though the derivations in the eigen-framework for test MSE are based on ideal Gaussianity).

In reality, the design matrix $X$ is only approximately Gaussian, not perfectly so. The simplest counterexample to ideal Gaussianity occurs when the domain $\mathcal{X}$ is finite. In that case, $X$ is a discrete random variable and therefore cannot be Gaussian. As a result, the claim that “$X$ is full rank” might occasionally fail with a very small probability—but in practice, this almost never happens. This is what we meant in our earlier response to reviewer HVtJ.

Now regarding the second comment. If I understood correctly, the expression you refer to uses the notation from Section 5.1, where $\mathcal{E}$ denotes the expected error of standard KRR (the same formula derived under the universality assumption in the eigen-framework). In our paper, however, $\hat{f}$ denotes the output of C-KRR. For the equality
$$
\mathcal{E} = \mathbb{E}\big[(\hat{f}(X) - f_{\parallel}(X))^2\big]
$$
to hold, $\hat{f}$ would have to be the output of standard KRR instead. So there is probably a minor notational confusion here.

I thank the authors for the clarifications, notably the inclusion of Fig. 7.

> Thank you for highlighting this interesting point. However, there is no inconsistency once the statements are interpreted within the “eigen-framework for KRR generalization”, the terminology you yourself used. Recall that this framework relies on the “universality assumption”,

Also, the fact that X is full rank does not seem to be true with probability 1 as far as I understand, albeit with high probability with $N$. However, I now understand the authors adapt a result from Simon et al, 2023.

> The cost of conditioning quantifies the squared $L_2$-distance between the estimator produced by C-KRR and the estimator obtained from $\mathcal{F}$-conditional learning. In subsection 5.1, we assume that the regression function lies in $\mathcal{F}$. Under this assumption, $\mathcal{F}$-conditional learning is, by definition, equivalent to applying standard KRR with the residual kernel to a dataset consisting only of noise, ${(X_i, \varepsilon_i)}_{i=1}^N$. This immediately yields that the expected risk of C-KRR is bounded by the expected risk of this noise-only KRR plus the cost of conditioning.

I am still confused. Naively, I would expect
$$
\mathcal{E}=\mathbb{E}[(\hat{f}(X)-f_{\parallel}(X))^2]=\mathbb{E}[(\hat{f}(X)-f_{\parallel}(X)-h(X))^2]-\mathbb{E}[h(X)^2]+2\mathbb{E}[(\hat{f}(X)-f_{\parallel}(X))h(X)]=c_{con}-\mathcal{E}^\prime+2\mathbb{E}[(\hat{f}(X)-f_{\parallel}(X))h(X)]
$$
Could the authors clarify further?

Thank you for your thoughtful feedback and valuable time.

Q1: “It seems that all the kernels …”

Many such examples are collected in Wendland (2004). One classical case is the thin-plate kernel $K(x,y)=(-1)^{k+1}|x-y|^{2k}\log|x-y|$,
which is CPD on $\mathbb{R}^d$ with respect to multivariate polynomials of degree $\le k$. Conditional KRR with this kernel is widely used to approximate surfaces in 3D from point clouds (or to interpolate them when $\lambda = +\infty$).

Another important example is
$K(x,y)=(-1)^{k+1}|x-y|^{2k+1}$,
defined for natural $k$, which is CPD on $\mathbb{R}^d$ with respect to polynomials of degree $\le k$. This kernel is closely related to the NNGP kernel of a two-layer neural network with activation $\mathrm{relu}(x)^k$; see (Bach, On the relationship between multivariate splines and infinitely-wide neural networks).


Q2: “Could you discuss the computational complexity of conditional KRR compared to standard KRR? Are there any additional computational costs associated with incorporating unpenalized features?”

The computationally most demanding step in Conditional KRR is solving the standard KRR problem with the empirical residual kernel (see Theorem 3). Thus, Conditional KRR does not introduce additional computational cost unless the number of unpenalized features $k$ becomes comparable to, or larger than, the sample size $N$. 

The first stage — linear regression on the features $f_1,\dots,f_k$ — is dominated by computing their empirical covariance matrix, which requires $\mathcal{O}(Nk^2)$ operations. Let $K=[K(X_i,X_j)]$ denote the empirical kernel matrix and let $K_{\mathrm{res}}$ be the empirical residual kernel matrix. If $\Pi$ is the projection operator onto the span of the vectors $[f_j(X_i)]_{i=1}^N)$ for 
$j=1,...,k$, then 

$K_{res} = (I - \Pi) K (I - \Pi)$.

A naive computation of $K_{\mathrm{res}}$ takes $\mathcal{O}(N^3)$. Solving the residual KRR problem in the second stage likewise requires $\mathcal{O}(N^3)$. Therefore, the overall complexity is dominated by the $\mathcal{O}(N^3)$ term—essentially the same as that of standard KRR when implemented naively.

In our implementation (see
https://github.com/anoniclr2026/scripts/blob/main/Conditioning%20Cost.py), we use this naive approach. Even if one employs a fast KRR method such as the Nyström approximation for $K$, obtaining a Nyström approximation of $K_{\mathrm{res}}$ from that of $K$ is straightforward. Hence, these acceleration techniques extend naturally to Conditional KRR, and we again conclude that its computational complexity remains close to that of standard KRR.

W1: All the topics listed above are for future work.

W2: “present illustrative settings for the conditional KRR to outperform standard KRR”

We have updated the manuscript to address this issue (which was also raised by other reviewers).

For a fixed regularization parameter $\lambda$, Figures 3, 4, and 8 in the previous version already showed that Conditional KRR outperforms standard KRR on both synthetic data and MNIST. In the revised version, we additionally include Figure 9, which demonstrates the same effect in the hard-thresholding setting for MNIST.

The situation is more subtle when KRR is tuned with the optimal regularization parameter $\lambda$. To clarify this case, we added Figure 7, which presents a synthetic example where Conditional KRR outperforms standard KRR for every choice of $\lambda$.

We also added a new subsection (H.3) devoted to experiments with hard thresholding on MNIST. The results, summarized in Table 1, show that the test MSE of C-KRR (in the hard-thresholding regime) and optimally tuned KRR are nearly identical.

Finally, we included a new Figure 10, comparing the test MSE of KRR with that of C-KRR using 20 unpenalized features pre-trained in advance. This figure illustrates that C-KRR outperforms standard KRR on MNIST when high-quality features are selected for $\mathcal{F}$.

W3: “Statistical significance of the results should also be reported”

The newly added plots report significance intervals corresponding to a 0.95 significance level.

summary.value:
This paper introduces and analyzes conditional Kernel Ridge Regression (KRR), an extension of standard KRR that incorporates unpenalized features from a function class $ \mathcal{F} $.
A conditionally positive definite (CPD) kernel $ K $ with respect to $ \mathcal{F} $ can be used for a two-stage learning process: linear regression on the features in $ \mathcal{F} $, followed by standard KRR on the residuals.
The paper proposes to construct residual kernel from a CPD kernel and use it to fit the residuals after regressing out the $ \mathcal{F} $-component.
The authors develop a theoretical framework to understand its statistical properties, reducing it to standard KRR with a "cost of conditioning" term.
Applications of the result to particular function classes $ \mathcal{F} $ are provided, including top eigenfunctions of the kernel and random features.
Empirical results are presented to demonstrate the performance of conditional KRR.

strengths.value:
* This paper is well-written and clearly structured, making it easy to follow the main ideas and contributions.
* The proposed theory on conditional KRR framework is novel. The theoretical analysis is rigorous, providing insights into the statistical properties of conditional KRR and its relationship to standard KRR.
* The applications to specific function classes, such as top eigenfunctions and random features, demonstrate the versatility of the proposed method.
* The empirical results partially validate the theoretical findings on the asymptotic behavior of conditional KRR.

weaknesses.value:
* Though a theory of the upper bound is provided, it seems that the upper bound is not very tight, especially when $\lambda$ is small (which is the case for KRR). The "cost of conditioning" term seems to be loose compared $k$-dimensional linear regression plus a standard KRR on the residuals.
Also, it would be helpful to provide minimax lower bounds.
* For the applications, it would be much clearer to present illustrative settings for the conditional KRR to outperform standard KRR. Moreover, some heuristic arguments are made in this section, but more rigorous analysis would be preferred.

* More experiments would be helpful to validate the effectiveness of conditional KRR, especially in real-world datasets. Statistical significance of the results should also be reported.
In addition, a comparison with classical KRR could be provided to demonstrate the advantages of conditional KRR.

summary.value: The authors propose a learning rule they term "conditional kernel ridge regression,"  which essentially consists of two steps: training a linear model on fixed features, and then training a kernel on the resulting residual. The final estimator is the sum of the estimators yielded by each step. They prove that an object called the residual kernel is PSD, and that the second step of CKRR is equivalent to KRR in the residual kernel's RKHS. Finally, they prove that the additional error incurred by using this two-step estimator decays as $1/\sqrt{N}$, though they empirically found a faster rate.

strengths.value: The two-stage learning rule is interesting, and may connect to other efforts to learn interpretable and transparent estimators. The authors' use of the KRR generalization eigen-framework in the analysis appears new to me.

weaknesses.value:
1) It is not clear to me that this learning rule is relevant to practice. It would be nice to empirically see a relevant setting (or, at least, any setting at all) in which conditional KRR outperforms optimally-regularized KRR. However, I'm not sure that it's possible to guarantee this -- since both learning stages are linear in the target, the cost or benefit of conditioning will depend on the alignment between the target, the residual kernel, and the chosen function class $\mathcal{F}$. (I believe this follows from the eigen-framework for KRR generalization.)
2) The role of L2 regularization in the first linear regression stage is not treated. 
3) The proposed quantity "cost of conditioning" seems like a misnomer, and it's not clear how to interpret it. The defined quantity presumes omniscient knowledge of the component of the target in $\mathcal{F}$, even though any learning rule will need to estimate this. I think a more informative quantity (which may deserve the name "cost of conditioning" more) is something like
$\| \hat f_{KRR} - \hat f_{CKRR; \mathcal{F}} \|$, i.e., the cost (or benefit!) of implementing the first conditional step rather than using KRR for the full estimation. This quantity can be understood in terms of the alignment metrics mentioned in point 1.
4) I found the experiments unconvincing and unclear. The top row of Fig 2 does not agree with the theoretical bound (the bound is too pessimistic). The bottom row is consistent with standard linear regression theory, and seems like a weak test of Theorem 4. Fig 3 is very confusing to me -- why is the estimator in the middle panel so bad? Usually KRR with optimal regularization is a pretty powerful estimator. The takeaway message for Fig 4 is unclear.
5) I believe there is an error in line 305 -- the test error should not vanish when the target noise vanishes. There will be leftover estimator variance from the sampling noise.

questions.value:
1) Why is it important to develop a statistical theory of learning for conditional KRR?
2) Does the first linear regression stage require using no ridge regularization?
3) Can you clarify the takeaway message regarding the analysis of hard-thresholded vs. soft-thresholded residual kernels?
4) Double descent (in linear learning rules) is known to be a pathology resulting from badly-chosen regularization. Do you expect the U-shaped curves to vanish if the regularization is chosen well in the second learning stage, or would the first linear regression learning stage interfere?

summary.value: The authors study conditional kernel ridge regression, which consists in linear regression along a set of unpenalized features F, plus KRR  using a residual kernel to estimate the orthogonal component. The authors first rigorously characterize the cost of conditioning, defined as the squared discrepancy between the corresponding estimator and an estimator with oracle knowledge of the component in F. They then apply the result to study thresholding, where the set of eigenmodes containing the target is less penalized, and derive a sufficient condition on the signal strength for conditional KRR to outperform usual KRR. This results in some cases in U-shaped curves for the test error as a function of the number of unpenalized features, which are illustrated in a number of experiments.

strengths.value: The paper provides a detailed study of the impact of conditioning on KRR. Their study sheds light on a number of interesting facts, notably by determining a sufficient condition (3) for thresholded KRR to outperform standard KRR, leading to interesting non-monotonic curves in the test error, as a function of the number unpenalized features. While I have very limited familiarity with the techniques used, and have not carefully checked the technical derivations, the results seem to the best of my reading sound and novel. I am thus in favor of acceptance; albeit with very low confidence.

weaknesses.value:
While the paper is overall clearly written, a minor criticism is that the current exposition is at points somewhat dense (for example Section 2), and the motivation of studying the problem would gain to be further expounded or reminded throughout technical sections. I would find it for instance helpful if the authors could motivate further applications of conditional KRR in the introduction. I would also think that moving the experiments on real data of Fig. 7 into the main text would strengthen the manuscript, and add an extra helpful illustration to the findings. 

Beside these points, I am listing some questions in the next section.

comment.value:
Thank you for your thoughtful and constructive review; your comments have helped us improve the manuscript.

“Remark 1 shows the equivalence between two-step procedure by the residual kernel and the direct estimation of conditional KRR by (1). What is benefit of this consequence?”

Our implementation of Conditional KRR follows Theorem 3, which provides a formal counterpart to Remark 1 (see also our response to reviewer oQxu regarding implementation). Remark 1 highlights the importance of the residual kernel; however, the residual kernel used in Theorem 3 is defined with respect to the empirical distribution rather than the true distribution $P$. This prevents Theorem 3 from being directly applied in the subsequent theoretical analysis, since the residual kernel is data-dependent rather than fixed. For this reason, additional analysis is needed—carried out in Section 4—where we eliminate this dependence on empirical data.

“What is the definition of the initial kernel K of Theorem 1?”

It is CPD w.r.t. $\mathcal{F}$, as we say in line 124. We will repeat this in the body of the theorem.

“Further, I do not understand why (2) is called as 'cost of conditioning'.”

The same question is asked by reviewer HVtJ (Weakness 3), so I refer to the discussion above.

“What does the constraint \sum_i \alpha_i f(x_i) = 0 imply? I do not have any intuition behind this constraint (in a practical scenario).” + “The residual kernel seemingly a central idea of the paper, but I even do not understand what it is for. What situation is this approach required or effective in what sense? A motivation should have been clarified in a clearer way.”


The condition $\sum_i \alpha_i f(x_i)=0$ simply means that the generalized function $g=\sum_i \alpha_i \delta_{x_i}$ is orthogonal to every $f\in\mathcal{F}$.
A kernel $K$ is CPD w.r.t. $\mathcal{F}$ precisely when, for any such ''generalized vector'' $g$ perpendicular to $\mathcal{F}$, the quadratic form $\iint g(x) K(x,y) g(y)dxdy\geq 0$. Intuitively, the kernel is positive definite on the subspace orthogonal to $\mathcal{F}$, while the kernel does not penalize the directions represented by $\mathcal{F}$ (because they will be eliminated by the first stage of conditional KRR). If we additionally fix some probabilistic measure $P$, Theorem 2 gives a deeper understanding of that condition.

Now to see better the idea of a residual kernel, let us consider the case of finite domain, i.e. $|\mathcal{X}|=n$. In that case, a positive definite kernel corresponds to an $n\times n$ positive definite matrix $K$. Such a matrix induces an inner product $x^\top K y$, i.e., a full Euclidean geometry (distances, angles, norms) on ${\mathbb R}^n$. For the CPD kernel w.r.t. $\mathcal{F}$, the finite version is a symmetric matrix $K$ such that the bilinear form $x^\top K y$ becomes an inner product only on the subspace orthogonal to $\mathcal{F}\subseteq {\mathbb R}^n$. Now, the simplest way to correspond full Euclidean geometry to $K$, is to define the bilinear form $x^\top (I-\Pi) K (I-\Pi) y$ where $\Pi$ is the projection operator onto $\mathcal{F}$. Then, $(I-\Pi) K (I-\Pi)$ is exactly the residual kernel.

Passing back to the infinite setting, where kernels are defined on an input domain ${\mathcal X}\subseteq {\mathbb R}^d$, we have the following correspondences between finite and infinite objects:

vectors from ${\mathbb R}^n$ --> functions $\mathcal{X}\to {\mathbb R}$

symmetric $n\times n$ matrix $K$ --> symmetric function $\mathcal{X}\times \mathcal{X}\to {\mathbb R}$

$\mathcal{F}\subseteq {\mathbb R}^n$ --> space of functions $\mathcal{F}$

PD matrix $K$ --> positive definite kernel $\mathcal{X}\times \mathcal{X}\to {\mathbb R}$

CPD matrix $K$ w.r.t. $\mathcal{F}\subseteq {\mathbb R}^n$ --> CPD kernel w.r.t. $\mathcal{F}$

$(I-\Pi) K (I-\Pi)$ --> residual kernel w.r.t. $\mathcal{F}$ (defined by $P$)

“Is f_|| a true function? Then, in what situation, 'learner has full access to the component f_||' is possible?”

Yes, $f_{\parallel}$ is a true function. The notion of $\mathcal{F}$-conditional learning is purely hypothetical—no learner is ever given the $\mathcal{F}$-component of the regression function in practice. Instead, conditional KRR attempts to recover this component from data during the first stage of learning.

The key point is that $\mathcal{F}$-conditional learning corresponds to standard KRR with a fixed kernel: the residual kernel defined by $\mathcal{F}$ and the true distribution $P$. The cost of conditioning quantifies how close practical conditional KRR is to this idealized standard KRR (which we refer to as $\mathcal{F}$-conditional learning).

The central purpose of Theorem 4 is to bound this cost. In other words, the “cost of conditioning” is the additional amount that must be added to the expected risk so that conditional KRR can be analyzed as if it were standard KRR with a fixed kernel.
